facts.text: Rigoletto had a triumphant premiere at La Fenice in Venice on 11 March 1851, after serious trouble with the Austrian censors.
facts.evidence: the opera had a triumphant premiere at La Fenice in Venice on 11 March 1851

facts.text: The source, Victor Hugo’s play Le roi s’amuse, had been banned in France after its premiere and wasn’t staged again until 1882.
facts.evidence: The play had been banned in France following its premiere nearly twenty years earlier (not to be staged again until 1882)

facts.text: Verdi told Piave to get permission at any cost: “Use four legs, run through the town and find me an influential person.”
facts.evidence: Use four legs, run through the town and find me an influential person

facts.text: Verdi on his hunchbacked jester: “There is a character that is one of the greatest creations that the theatre can boast of.”
facts.evidence: there is a character that is one of the greatest creations that the theatre can boast of

facts.text: The censor flatly refused “La Maledizione” (the working title). One rewrite turned the king into a duke and dropped both the hunchback and the curse; Verdi refused it.
evidence: the Austrian censor De Gorzkowski emphatically denied consent to the production of "La Maledizione"
in which the sovereign was a duke and both the hunchback and the curse disappeared
Verdi was completely against this proposed solution

facts.text: The jester was originally called Triboulet. The name Rigoletto came from a parody comedy, “Rigoletti, or The last of the jesters”.
facts.evidence: renamed Rigoletto from a parody of a comedy

facts.sceneMatch: Della mia bella|Questa o quella|^Act I$
facts.text: At the premiere, Felice Varesi (Rigoletto) froze in panic. Verdi pushed him onstage, and he tumbled on clumsily; the audience thought it was a planned gag.
evidence: he had a panic attack when it was his turn to enter the stage
roughly pushed him on the stage, so he appeared with a clumsy tumble
The audience, thinking it was an intentional gag, was very amused.

facts.sceneMatch: La donna è mobile|La donna e mobile
facts.text: Verdi kept “La donna è mobile” secret until a few hours before the premiere and forbade anyone to sing or whistle it outside the theatre.
facts.evidence: forbidding them to sing, whistle or even think of the melody outside of the theatre

facts.sceneMatch: La donna è mobile|La donna e mobile
facts.text: The morning after the premiere, “La donna è mobile” was being sung in the streets.
facts.evidence: which was sung in the streets the next morning

facts.text: Because of censorship, Rigoletto sometimes played in Italy under other names, such as Viscardello, Lionello and Clara de Perth.
facts.evidence: e.g. as Viscardello, Lionello, and Clara de Perth

facts.text: “Zitti, zitti” (“Softly, softly”): blindfolded and tricked, Rigoletto holds the ladder while the courtiers abduct his own daughter.
facts.evidence: Blindfolded and deceived, he holds the ladder steady while they climb up to Gilda's room

facts.text: The courtiers gleefully tell the Duke they have captured “Rigoletto’s mistress”. It is really Gilda, his daughter.
Verdi finished the score on 5 February 1851, little more than a month before the premiere.
facts.evidence: Verdi finally completed the composition on 5 February 1851, a little more than a month before the premiere.
